title: Writing the note
objectives: Write the replication note, including what did not survive.

screens.title: The note's key line
screens.prose: The note this lesson writes replicates Gatev, Goetzmann and Rouwenhorst (2006) on our seeded panel. Its key line answers the curriculum's question: how much of the effect survived? Take the top 5 with the wait.
screens.question: What share of the top 5's waited return survived the break?

hints.text: After over before.
About 69%.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide after by before.

explain.text: 0.88% / 1.28% is about 69%. The top 20 keep 42%, because the three unbroken pairs usually rank in the top 5 after the break. The note reports both, led by the top 20.

screens.title: A draft note
screens.prose: A colleague's draft summary. Every number is right. One line claims more than our data can show.

lines: Top 20, wait a day: 0.75% a month, 9.4% a year.
Same day on closes: 1.00% a month; part is bounce.
After the break: 0.48% a month against 1.14% before.
Pairs trading still works on real markets today.
Engle-Granger selection: 0.63% a month on 22 cycles.
params.title: draft-note.md

screens.question: Tap the line that overclaims.

feedback.correct: Correct. A seeded panel says nothing about real markets.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the line that draws a conclusion the panel cannot support.

byKey.l5: That line reports the decline with both halves. It is honest.
byKey.l2: That line reports the conservative cell, annualised. It is honest.

explain.text: Line 6 turns results on planted data into a claim about markets. Every other line reports a number and how it was made. We put the pairs in ourselves, so their profits prove only that the code works.

screens.title: The results in numbers
screens.prose: Fill in the note's derived figures from the level's results, for the top 20 with the wait. Give each as a percentage.
screens.question: Complete the four cells.

hints.text: A month is a sixth of a cycle; a year compounds twelve months.
Survival is after over before.
Break-even is the per-cycle return over 4 × round trips.

feedback.correct: Correct. The four figures the note quotes.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check each cell's rule.

byKey.x6: You multiplied by 6. A month is a sixth of a cycle.
byKey.simple: You multiplied by 12. Compound the twelve months.
byKey.once: You charged one trade per round trip. Each round trip is four £1 trades.

explain.text: 4.52% / 6 = 0.75% a month, and (1 + 0.0075)¹² − 1 = 9.4% a year. 0.48% / 1.14% gives 42% survived. 4.52% / (4 × 1.6886) = 0.67% per trade breaks even.

screens.title: The survival sentence
screens.prose: The extension section needs one sentence. The paper's rules, top 20 with the wait, earn 1.14% a month before the break and 0.48% after.
screens.question: Which sentence should the note use?

options.text: With the paper's rules unchanged, about 42% of the waited top-20 return survived the planted break
Pairs trading died after publication
options.why: 42% survived, and on planted data. The sentence overclaims twice.

options.text: Returns fell by 0.66 points a month
options.why: True, but it leaves out the share, which is what the curriculum asks.

options.text: Our best held-out cell earned 1.20% a month
options.why: That cell was chosen on the held-out half.

hints.text: The curriculum asks how much survived.
Give a share, the rules and the data.
About 42%, rules unchanged, planted break.

feedback.generic: Not quite. The sentence needs the share, the rules and the data.

explain.text: The sentence gives the share, 42%, the untuned rules and the planted cause. A reader can check each part. The points figure and the tuned cells come after it.

screens.title: What changes on real data
screens.prose: The note ends with what a run on real shares would face. With 5,000 shares there are 12,497,500 pairs, about 2,525 times our 4,950.

rows: Our cells beside the paper's facts
Why profits fell, and the evidence
One look; the share that survived
What the seeded panel cannot show

screens.question: Which belong in that paragraph? Select all that apply.

options.text: Delistings, mergers and other corporate actions
Dividends, which a total-return index must include
Short-sale fees and recalls on the short leg
Bid-ask spreads that vary by share and by year
Pairs that break for reasons a seeded break cannot imitate, and no list of true pairs
A different distance formula
options.why: The sum of squared differences is the same on real data.

options.text: No need for the one-day wait
options.why: Real closes sit at the bid or the ask too, so the wait still matters.

hints.text: Ask what our generator left out.
It has no dividends, delistings, borrow fees or varying spreads.
And it tells us which pairs are real.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Pick what our generator does not model.

explain.text: Our generator has fixed spreads, no dividends, no delistings and no borrow fees. It also tells us which pairs are real, which no real dataset does. Each gap moves real results in a direction the note should state.

screens.title: The headline number
screens.prose: A colleague's note leads with 1.50% a month: the top 20, same day, before the break, before costs.
screens.question: What is wrong with that headline?

options.text: It stacks the three most flattering choices: same-day fills, no costs and only the years before the break
Nothing, if the method section explains it
options.why: You trusted the method section to undo the headline. Readers quote the headline.

options.text: It should be annualised first
options.why: Annualising changes the units, not the flattering choices.

options.text: It uses committed capital
options.why: Committed capital is the conservative return; employed is higher.

hints.text: List the choices behind the figure.
Fill, costs and years.
Each is the flattering one.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Check each choice behind the figure.

byKey.b: You let the method section carry the caveats. The headline is what readers repeat.

explain.text: 1.50% takes the same-day fill, no costs and the pre-break years. The conservative lead is 0.75% a month with the wait, over all years. Costs and the decline sit beside it.

screens.title: When nothing survives
screens.prose: Edge case. Suppose the held-out half had earned −0.05% a month against 1.14% before.
screens.question: What should the note do?

options.text: Say that none of the effect survived, with the same prominence and the same method
Try other thresholds on the held-out half until one is positive
options.why: That chooses on the held-out half, which makes it in sample.

options.text: Leave the extension out, since the replication matched
options.why: The extension is what the curriculum asks for. A null result is a result.

options.text: Report the in-sample figure instead
options.why: That hides the answer to the question the note sets.

hints.text: What did the note set out to measure?
How much survived.
Report the answer, whatever it is.

feedback.generic: Not quite. A null extension is still the answer.

explain.text: −0.05 / 1.14 is negative, so the line reads "None of the effect survived". It sits where the 42% would have. Readers trust a note that reports a failure as plainly as a success.

screens.title: The note in order
screens.prose: Put the note's sections in the order a reader needs them. The cointegration and factor sections may come either way round.
screens.question: Order the sections.

lines.text: Question and paper: the distance method and its claim
Data: the seeded panel, what it plants and why
Method: normalise, distance, top 20, 2 sd, crossings, the wait, both capitals
Results against the paper's quoted facts
The decline and its planted cause
Out of sample: how much survived
What failed, and what changes on real data

hints.text: A reader needs the question and data before any result.
Results and costs come before the critiques.
The extension and the real-data caveats close the note.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Question, data and method come first; caveats last.

explain.text: The note runs from what was asked, through how and what we found, to what it means. The decline comes before the out-of-sample test, which measures it once. The real-data paragraph closes, because it bounds every claim above it.

screens.title: The survival line in code
screens.prose: Turn two means into the note's sentence. A ratio of zero or below reads "None of the effect survived". With no in-sample effect there is nothing to survive, so raise `ValueError`.
screens.question: Complete `survival_sentence(pre, post)`.

widget.starter:
def survival_sentence(pre, post):
    """The note's survival line from the in-sample and held-out means."""
    ratio = post / pre
    return f"{round(100 * ratio)}% of the effect survived"
widget.how: Submit runs 7 hidden tests. Two are real splits; the rest cover a loss, a zero, two empty in-sample cases and a rise.

hints.text: Check pre first.
Then compute the ratio and check its sign.
Round 100 × ratio to a whole number.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Handle a non-positive pre, then a non-positive ratio.

explain.text: 0.0048 / 0.0114 gives 42%. A rise above the in-sample figure reads over 100%, as with 3 sd and k = 5. A zero in-sample mean raises, because a share of nothing is undefined.

screens.title: The README and the interview
screens.prose: Your replication is on GitHub. An interviewer asks: "Tell me about it in two sentences."
screens.question: Which answer is soundest?

options.text: On a seeded panel I replicated the distance method, matching the paper's range at 0.75% a month. Held out after a planted break, about 42% survived, because fewer pairs converged.
I proved pairs trading still beats the market by 9% a year.
options.why: A seeded panel proves nothing about markets, and 9% is the in-sample figure.

options.text: My best setting made 1.97% a month in years 1 to 6.
options.why: That is the most flattering cell of a sweep.

options.text: I wrote a backtester with many settings and a good Sharpe ratio.
options.why: It says nothing about the paper, the data or what survived.

hints.text: Name the method, the data, the match and the survival.
Keep the conservative cell.
Add the cause of the decline.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Give the method, the data, the conservative match and what survived.

explain.text: The answer names the method and admits the data is seeded. It gives the conservative figure, the share that survived and the cause. The README's first lines should say the same.

ideas: The note runs from question, data and method through results, costs and the decline to the extension and its limits.
Lead with the conservative cell, 0.75% a month with the wait. The key line is the share that survived: about 42%.
Report a failure as plainly as a success, and say what a seeded panel cannot show.
